what_it_does: Running a large language model (an AI that generates text) requires repeatedly loading enormous tables of numbers from main memory (slow off-chip DRAM chips) and doing relatively little arithmetic on them — this is called 'memory-bound' behavior — but at other times the same model needs intense number-crunching with less memory pressure, called 'compute-bound' behavior. The mix shifts depending on how many requests are being handled at once and how long the conversation has gotten. Rather than picking one type of processor and accepting bad performance for the opposite case, PAPI combines two kinds of processing units in one system: math-first units (similar to a GPU) for compute-heavy moments, and computing-inside-memory units (processors built directly into the memory chips so data does not have to travel far) for memory-heavy moments. A runtime monitor watches each AI operation as it arrives and routes it to whichever processing unit is currently best suited, adapting dynamically as the workload characteristics shift.
